Stage 01
01

The Filter.
Their question, not yours.

Before you build your argument, identify the filter. The same information lands completely differently depending on which question the other person is unconsciously asking.

Financial Filter
CFO · Head of Finance
“Does this affect the number I report to the board?”
How to recognise it
Asks for data before anything else. Interrupts narratives with numbers. Uses phrases like "what is the ROI on this" and "how does this show up on the P&L."
Never open with
"This person is really important to us." Cannot act on that.
Opens the filter
"I want to show you a cost-benefit. The numbers are straightforward."
Operational Filter
COO · Head of Operations
“Does this break something that is currently working?”
How to recognise it
Thinks in processes and connected systems. Wants the implementation plan before the strategy. Asks "who owns this" and "what is the timeline."
Never open with
"We are still figuring out the details." Ambiguity is their enemy.
Opens the filter
"I have a plan and I need your operational perspective before I move."
Political Filter
Senior Director · MD
“Does this strengthen or expose me?”
How to recognise it
Reads every request for hidden agenda. Thinks about how it looks to peers and to the CEO. Protects their territory fiercely.
Never open with
"I want to share something I heard about your team." Too direct, too fast.
Opens the filter
"I want your perspective before I draw any conclusions. You know this context better than anyone."
Strategic Filter
CEO · Founder
“Does this move us toward or away from what I am building?”
How to recognise it
Thinks in 3 to 5 year horizons. Connects everything to the big picture. Loses interest when conversations feel like daily operations or defensive responses.
Never open with
"This is an HR process we need to run." Process language closes CEOs.
Opens the filter
"This has a direct impact on our ability to scale the team we need."
Relational Filter
CHRO · HR Manager · Peer
“Does this come from someone I trust, and does it make me look good or bad?”
How to recognise it
Decides based on relationship history as much as data. Sensitive to being bypassed or surprised. Needs to feel like a partner, not a recipient.
Never open with
"I already spoke to the CEO about this." They needed to be first.
Opens the filter
"I wanted to bring this to you first before anything else moves."
McKinsey · Influence Research · 2022
72% of failed internal proposals are rejected not because the idea was wrong, but because they were framed for the wrong filter.
The data was correct. The logic was sound. The filter was misread.
Use this
"Before I present this. What would make this easy for you to say yes to?"
Works in: any stakeholder meeting before you present a proposal
Read the filter in 60 seconds

Each person below opens with one sentence. What filter does it reveal?

Adriano Mendes · Director of Research
Adriano Mendes says
"I want to understand why you are speaking to my team before speaking to me. That is not how things work here."
Political Filter
His first concern is not what you found. It is that you went around him. "That is not how things work here" is political filter language. He is protecting his domain. The content of the conversation does not matter yet. The process does.
Opens this filter"You are right. I should have come to you first. Let me explain why I did not, and then share what I found."
Carlos Oliveira · COO · Valore Bank
Carlos Oliveira says
"I have 15 minutes. Tell me what is happening on Adriano's team, what you have done about it, and what you need from me."
Operational Filter
"What is happening / what have you done / what do you need". This is the operational filter in pure form: status, action, owner. He is not asking how people feel. He is asking where things stand.
Opens this filterLead with status. Follow with a specific ask. Do not open with context or background.
CEO · Valore Bank
CEO says
"I got Adriano's email. Before I decide anything, tell me what this means for the bank's research capability over the next 12 months."
Strategic Filter
He skipped the conflict entirely and went straight to the future. That is the strategic filter: he is not judging who is right, he is asking what this costs the bank going forward.
Opens this filter"In the next 12 months, if this pattern continues, we lose the analytical talent that produces our flagship research. Here is how we resolve it."
Priya Nair · Senior Research Analyst
Priya Nair says
"I need to know: is what I told you going to come back to me? Because I trusted you with that."
Relational Filter
She is not asking about the outcome. She is asking whether the trust she extended was safe. Do not reassure her with process. Reassure her with specifics.
Opens this filter"What you told me stays as a theme. I will never say your name or quote you directly. You have my word on that specifically."
Your turn · Valore BankIdentify the filter
The Adriano situation needs to reach the CEO. Before writing a single word. What filter does the CEO of Valore Bank use? What does that mean for the first sentence?
Adriano says
"My team delivers. Our research goes to the largest clients in this bank."
What question is the CEO unconsciously asking, and how does your opening sentence answer that question first?
Reference
The CEO uses a strategic filter: "Does this threaten what I am building?" He is not asking if Adriano is a bad manager. He is asking if this situation threatens the bank's competitive capability.

"I want to flag something affecting our ability to retain the analytical talent that underpins our research capability, and I want your view on how we handle it."

Not: "I have a complaint about a director." That is HR process language. Strategic filter language connects to capability and the future.
The filter tells you the first sentence. The first sentence sets the frame for everything that follows.
Stage 02
02

The Timing.
Same proposal. Different moment.

The filter tells you how to frame it. The timing tells you when the window is open, at two levels: organisational and interpersonal.

Organisational window
Window open
The conditions are right
  • Start of a new budget cycle or fiscal quarter
  • New leader recently appointed, still building their agenda
  • A recent visible failure that created urgency
  • The team just lost someone important. The pain is fresh.
  • A competitor move that made the status quo feel risky
Window closed
Wait, or change your angle completely
  • Active crisis consuming leadership attention
  • A decision on this topic was just made
  • Political conflict between key stakeholders is unresolved
  • Budget is frozen or under review
  • The person you need just returned from leave
Harvard Business Review · Decision Timing · 2021
Proposals presented during organisational transition moments are 2.4× more likely to be approved.
A new leader, a recent failure, a team departure. These are decision windows. Strategic HR reads these moments as opportunities.
Use this
"I want to bring this to you now because the window for a clean outcome is still open."
Works in: opening a difficult conversation with a CEO or COO
Your turn · Valore BankRead the window
It is Thursday afternoon. Felipe filed his complaint Tuesday. Adriano knows you spoke to Gabriel and Priya. Carlos is available this afternoon. The CEO has a board meeting Monday. What do you do in the next 4 hours, and why?
Name what you do, in what order, and why Thursday afternoon is different from Friday morning.
Reference
Window: open, and closing fast.

1. Brief Carlos this afternoon. 20 minutes. Not asking him to act. Making sure he is not surprised.
2. Send Adriano a calendar invite for tomorrow morning. Use a neutral subject line. Do not give him the weekend to prepare.
3. Prepare a one-page pattern summary for the CEO. Not to send yet, but ready if Adriano escalates.

Why Thursday and not Friday: Friday afternoon is when people mentally check out. A difficult conversation on Friday has no resolution before Monday, which is the board meeting, making everything more political.
"The window for a clean outcome is still open, but only just."
Interpersonal window · Reading the room

The organisational window can be open, and the interpersonal window still closed. Before you approach anyone, read the person in that moment.

Closed
grumpy
mal-humorado
Irritable and bad-tempered. Small things bother them more than usual.
"The CEO was grumpy all morning after the board call. Not the day to ask for a budget exception."
short-tempered
com o pavio curto
Easily annoyed and quick to react with frustration.
"She has been short-tempered since the deal fell through. Read that before you walk in."
preoccupied
cabeça em outro lugar
Mentally focused on something else, physically present but not really listening.
"He seemed preoccupied during the meeting. Whatever I said, it was not landing."
to go through a rough patch
passando por um momento difícil
Experiencing a difficult period, professionally or personally.
"The CFO is going through a rough patch with the board. This is not the week to escalate."
distracted
distraído
Unable to concentrate. Attention is elsewhere.
"She kept checking her phone. Distracted. I rescheduled."
not in a good headspace
cabeça não está boa
Mentally not in the right place to engage with a difficult conversation.
"I could tell he was not in a good headspace. I kept it brief and said I'd follow up tomorrow."
Open
approachable
acessível
Easy to talk to in this moment. Open body language, unhurried.
"She was by the coffee machine, relaxed. Approachable. I took the opportunity."
in a good headspace
num bom estado mental
Mentally clear and ready to engage, present and focused.
"Catch him right after a win. That's when he's in the best headspace for new proposals."
receptive
receptivo
Willing to listen and consider new ideas without immediate resistance.
"She seemed receptive after the team presentation. I used that window."
to catch someone at a good time
pegar alguém num bom momento
To approach someone when they happen to be available and in the right state.
"I caught him at a good time: just after lunch, door open, no back-to-back meetings."

Six real moments. Open, closed, or wait?

Your CEO walks past you in the corridor without making eye contact. You have been waiting three days to raise the Adriano situation.
× Wrong moment
No eye contact is a signal: he is not available right now. Stopping him in the corridor in that state is a low-probability move. You will get a distracted response at best.
Use"I will find you when you have a moment." Then let him go.
Why?
What signal would change your read? If the CEO had slowed down, made brief eye contact, or said your name as he passed, the read shifts. No signal at all is the key indicator here.
The CFO stops to make coffee at 10am and starts chatting with a colleague. You have a quick budget question pending for a week.
✓ Right moment
He stepped away from his desk, which means he stepped away from whatever was consuming him. He is approachable and in a social mode.
Use"Rafael, while I have you: quick question on the Q3 budget line. Two minutes?"
Why?
What would make this the wrong moment? If he was on his phone while making coffee, or if you knew he had a critical meeting in 10 minutes, the window would be narrower. Context within context.
You can hear raised voices from behind the COO's closed door. The meeting has been going for 90 minutes. You need his sign-off before end of day.
↻ Wait
A closed door with tension behind it: do not knock. Wait until the door opens, then give him 10 minutes to decompress.
Use"Whenever you're free. I need 5 minutes before EOD on the Valore sign-off."
Why?
When might knocking be right? If your sign-off is truly urgent and missing the deadline has serious consequences, a brief knock with "I am sorry to interrupt, I need 60 seconds" can work. But it is high-risk.
Your CEO just came out of a presentation that went exceptionally well. The team is celebrating in the hallway.
✓ Right moment
A public win puts people in an expansive, receptive state. This is one of the best interpersonal windows that exists.
Use"Congratulations. I have something I'd love to run by you this week when you have a moment."
Why?
What would close this window? If the CEO is surrounded by board members or senior clients, the social context makes it inappropriate. Proximity to power changes the read.
The Director you need has been short-tempered all week. On Friday afternoon, he stops by your desk and asks about your weekend.
✓ Right moment
He initiated casual contact. This is a deliberate signal of availability. When someone short-tempered chooses small talk, the tension has passed.
UseRespond warmly, then: "Actually, do you have two minutes? I've been wanting to catch you."
Why?
What if it is a trap? Sometimes people in conflict make small talk to gather information. The signal to watch: is he asking questions, or just chatting? Questions signal agenda. Chat signals availability.
You find out the CHRO just received difficult feedback from the board about HR performance. You have a new initiative to propose.
× Wrong moment
She is in a rough patch and her first need is to process, not to evaluate new proposals. A new initiative right now lands as additional pressure.
Use"I heard the board session was tough. If there's anything I can do to help with the response, I'm here." The proposal can wait a week.
Why?
When might you proceed anyway? If your initiative is directly relevant to solving the board's concern, framing it that way changes the conversation. "I have something that might actually help with what the board raised" is different from proposing something new.
Window open
  • Door is open, or they stepped away from their desk
  • They initiated contact, even small talk
  • Relaxed body language, unhurried movement
  • Just came from a positive meeting or a win
  • Standing with coffee, in a social moment
  • They made eye contact and smiled as you passed
  • Mid-morning or just after lunch. Not end of day
Window closed
  • No eye contact, fast walk, looking at phone
  • Door closed, especially with voices behind it
  • Just came out of a tense or long meeting
  • Visibly distracted, checking messages mid-conversation
  • Short answers, minimal engagement
  • Something difficult happened today
  • Friday afternoon or end of a heavy week
Stage 03
03

The Sequence.
Who first. Then who.

The filter tells you how to frame it. The timing tells you when the window is open. The sequence tells you in what order to move because who you speak to first determines what every subsequent conversation looks like.

The Valore Bank sequence · This week
1
Carlos Oliveira
COO · Your structural ally
Brief Carlos first. He has access to the CEO and has already seen the pattern. You are not asking him to act. You are asking him to be informed. If Adriano escalates, Carlos is the wall that stops it.
2
The Data Package
Prepare before any conversation
Three exit interviews + Felipe's complaint + attrition data vs other teams. Pattern, not anecdote. Something that cannot be dismissed as one person's experience.
3
Adriano Mendes
Director of Research & Analytics
Face Adriano with the data after Carlos is informed. He will try to escalate. He cannot if Carlos already knows. End with a next step he owns.
4
The CEO · If needed
Only if Adriano refuses to engage
You do not go to the CEO first. By then, you have Carlos, the data, and a documented conversation. You arrive with a solved problem, not a complaint.
Kotter · Leading Change
Successful organisational interventions almost always have a coalition of sponsors built before the formal proposal is made.
The decision is rarely made in the room where it is presented. It is made in the conversations that happen before that room.
Use this
"Before I bring this to the CEO, I want to make sure you are in the loop. Your perspective matters to how this lands."
Works in: briefing a structural ally before a formal leadership conversation
The internal sponsor. What they are and why you need one
An internal sponsor is not someone who agrees with you. It is someone with formal authority who is willing to be known as supporting your position before the decision happens.

Carlos Oliveira is not a friend. He is a structural ally. A friend supports you privately. A structural ally is willing to be publicly associated with the outcome.
What a sponsor does
→Opens doors you cannot open alone
→Absorbs escalation. The threat to go to the CEO loses power
→Gives your data credibility and authority
→Is present in conversations where you are not
Your turn · Activate CarlosBrief your structural ally
There are 20 minutes with Carlos before the Adriano meeting. He needs to be informed, available if Adriano escalates, and not intervening prematurely. Write the opening and the specific ask.
Carlos says
"What is this about? Adriano told me you have been speaking to his team without telling him."
He already knows something. Be direct about what you did and why. Then make the specific ask.
Reference
"Carlos, you are right. I spoke to two members of Adriano's team as part of a climate assessment. I want to be transparent about what I found and why I am coming to you first.

I have heard consistent themes around recognition and authorship across three independent sources, including a formal complaint. I am meeting Adriano tomorrow to address it directly. I am not asking you to intervene.

What I am asking: if Adriano goes to the CEO before I have had a chance to close this: can I count on you to hold that conversation for 48 hours while I resolve it? That is all I need."

The specific ask: not "support me." "Hold the escalation for 48 hours" is specific, time-bound, and easy to say yes to.
"Hold the escalation for 48 hours." Specific asks get specific answers.
Final challenge · All three toolsFilter + Timing + Sequence
It is Monday. Adriano refused to engage on Friday. He sent the CEO an email over the weekend calling the HR assessment "an overreach." The CEO forwarded it to you with one line: "Can we talk?"

What filter does the CEO use? Is the window open or closed? Who do you brief before you respond, and what do you say in the first 30 seconds of the call?
Adriano moved first. You have 10 minutes to prepare. Filter → Timing → Sequence.
Reference
Filter: Strategic: "Does this threaten what I am building?" The CEO is not asking who is right. He is asking if this costs him something bigger.

Timing: Open, but narrow. He reached out to you, not to HR process. He is still forming his view.

Before you call: Text Carlos in 15 seconds: "CEO got Adriano's email. Calling him now." Carlos is not surprised.

First 30 seconds: "I am glad you reached out. I want to give you the full picture. Not just Adriano's version. I have three independent data points, a formal complaint, and a direct conversation where I offered a path to resolve this without it becoming a formal process. He chose not to take it. I think we can still close this cleanly, and I want to show you how."
"I think we can still close this cleanly, and I want to show you how." You arrive with a solution. That is Strategic HR.
